content.text: With tool calling, the model never executes anything. It replies with a structured request, a

block naming a tool and its arguments, and stops. Your code runs the function, sends the result back and calls the model again. That loop is yours, and so are validation, permissions and every side effect.

The logs show nothing, because the code printed the model's text and returned. The refund never ran. The model can't run it: it had asked the application to, and nobody answered.
"With function calling, the LLM executes my code or calls my API by itself." It's an easy picture to form:

items.text: The names suggest it. "Function calling" and "tool use" sound like the model is the one calling.
Chat products seem to act: assistants search the web, run code and edit files, and you never see who did the work.
SDK helpers hide the loop. Anthropic's SDKs include a tool runner, in beta, that runs your functions when Claude calls them, so the round trips are invisible.
Some tools really do run without your code: Anthropic runs server tools such as web search and code execution on its own infrastructure.

content.text: The half-truth: tools do let a model cause actions in the world. But the model's only output is tokens. Some program, yours or Anthropic's, reads the request, runs the operation and feeds the result back. The model never touches your database.
The model writes a request and stops

as a contract: you specify which operations exist and what shape their inputs take, and Claude decides when to call them. In their words, "The model never runs anything on its own." When Claude wants your tool, the response has

object that follows your schema. That's the entire action on the model's side: a JSON request inside a reply. As the Understanding LLMs path showed, a model predicts tokens; a tool call is tokens in a structured shape.

content.text: it answers. The results must come right after the assistant message that asked for them, and before any text in that user message. When Claude calls several tools at once, all the results go back together in one user message. And since the API is stateless, each round trip resends the whole conversation.
Research systems work the same way

This isn't an API quirk. Toolformer, a 2023 model from Meta AI trained to insert API calls into its own text, still needed the decoding to stop: when the model produced the token meaning "the API's response goes here", generation was interrupted, the API was called, and decoding continued with the response inserted. ReAct prompted models to interleave reasoning with actions such as
against a simple Wikipedia API, and the environment's observation was added before the next step. In both, the model proposes and a harness executes.
Server tools: someone else runs the loop

, Anthropic's servers run the operation and feed the output back to the model before the response reaches you. That's where "the model ran a search" comes from: the same contract, with Anthropic's code as the executor. That loop has an iteration limit, and when it's reached the response ends with
; you re-send the conversation to let Claude continue.
The definition is all the model knows

Claude never receives your implementation, only the schema you provide and the result you return. So the definition is your real interface. The docs call detailed descriptions "by far the most important factor in tool performance" and suggest at least 3–4 sentences: what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means and its limits. Adding
guarantees that Claude's inputs match your schema. That guarantees the shape of a call, not that the call is allowed.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=[REFUND_TOOL],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Refund order 1042, please."}],
)
# Prints "I'll refund order 1042 now." and nothing is refunded:
# stop_reason is "tool_use" and the request is never answered.
print(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))

Arguments come from the model, and tool results often carry content you don't control, such as web pages or inbound email, that can hide instructions aimed at Claude. That's
. Validate every argument, take identity and permissions from your session, and require a human's confirmation before irreversible actions. Anthropic also advises keeping untrusted content inside
blocks, not in the system prompt.

content.text: Check the arguments, the caller's permissions and your business rules in code before executing. Treat the model like an untrusted client of your own API.
Read-only tools can run automatically. Refunds, deletions and outgoing emails should need a confirmation step, or run in a dry-run mode first.
